passage: Aditi, you know how I used to redo every assignment till three in the morning? This semester I tried something my counsellor suggested. For the history essay, I set a timer for forty-five minutes and wrote a rough draft, full of gaps, no editing allowed. It felt awful, like walking out with my shirt inside out. Then I asked myself, what's the worst if this essay is mostly there instead of perfect? Honestly? A B-plus. I'd survive. So I did one round of edits and submitted it. Got an A-minus. The anxiety's still around, which is why I still see the counsellor every fortnight. But I sleep now. Me, Salma, asleep by midnight!

qa.q: How long did Salma set the timer for?
qa.a: Salma set it for forty-five minutes.

qa.q: How did Salma feel writing the rough draft, and what shows it?
qa.a: Salma felt very uncomfortable, like walking out with a shirt on inside out.

qa.q: What turning point helped Salma finish the essay?
qa.a: Asking what the worst would be if it wasn't perfect, and seeing it was only a B-plus, let Salma do one round of edits and submit.

qa.q: How might Aditi feel hearing that Salma now sleeps by midnight?
qa.a: Aditi probably feels glad and relieved, having known Salma used to stay up till three.

grounding: A student uses a time limit, a rough first draft and a worst-case question to finish work, and keeps seeing a counsellor for the anxiety.

passage: I'm Dolma, Asif's lab partner this year. He used to rewrite our lab reports five times and miss deadlines. This term I've watched him change. He sets his phone timer for one hour, writes a rough version, and then stops. Stops! Last week he deliberately handed in a report with the graph colours not matching, which would have killed him in August. His hand hovered over the submit button for a long time, then he clicked. He also mentioned, quickly, that he's been talking to the campus counsellor about the anxiety. I don't know how hard it is inside his head. But he laughs more in the lab now.

qa.q: How long is Asif's timer?
qa.a: He sets his phone timer for one hour.

qa.q: What does Asif's hand hovering over the submit button suggest?
qa.a: It suggests he felt anxious about sending imperfect work, even while choosing to do it.

qa.q: Which practice is helping Asif most, and why?
qa.a: Setting a time limit, writing a rough version and deliberately sending small flaws builds his tolerance, while the counsellor helps with the anxiety.

qa.q: How might the lab teacher see Asif's reports now?
qa.a: The teacher probably notices them arriving on time, which matters more than matching graph colours.

grounding: A lab partner watches a student use time limits, rough drafts and small deliberate imperfections, with a counsellor's support for his anxiety.

passage:
Week one, a Tuesday: Kiran set a phone timer for forty-five minutes and wrote the ugliest first draft of an essay she'd ever allowed herself. When the alarm rang, she stopped, mid-sentence.
Week two, a Friday: Stuck again on one paragraph, she asked herself Aparna's question: what if this was only ninety percent of my best? Would anyone notice? She submitted it with one clumsy sentence left in. Her hands shook a little.
Week five, a Monday: The essay came back with a B-plus. Kiran felt a stab of disappointment, then relief. She told Aparna the worry still woke her at night, and that afternoon they booked a slot with the college counsellor.

qa.q: How long was Kiran's timer?
qa.a: Forty-five minutes.

qa.q: How did Kiran feel when the B-plus came back?
qa.a: She felt a stab of disappointment, then relief.

qa.q: Which strategies helped Kiran finish?
qa.a: A time limit, a rough first draft and asking what ninety percent would look like, plus seeing a counsellor when the worry kept waking her.

qa.q: How might Aparna feel when Kiran shares that the worry still wakes her?
qa.a: Aparna likely feels concerned but glad Kiran is honest, and supportive in booking the counsellor.

grounding: Shows over weeks a young adult using time limits, rough drafts and a ninety-percent question, and seeking support for lasting worry.

passage: Gautam, sit. You remind me of myself at twenty, redrawing the same bridge plan till the paper went soft. My teacher at the polytechnic, old Mr Fernandes, took the pencil away. "One hour. Rough version. Then we see." I, Asif, argued. He tapped the clock. The rough version had mistakes, but it stood up. He asked me, "If this is ninety percent of your dream, will the bridge fall?" It wouldn't. So I started making small, deliberate imperfections: sending a letter with one typo, leaving a drawing a bit unfinished. It was agony at first. And when the worry kept me up for weeks, I spoke to a doctor. That was hard too, admitting I needed help. Now I finish things.

qa.q: Who took the pencil away?
qa.a: Old Mr Fernandes, the teacher at the polytechnic.

qa.q: What was young Asif feeling when asked to make a rough version?
qa.a: Asif felt resistant and anxious, arguing because anything less than perfect felt wrong.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the story?
qa.a: Mr Fernandes's question about ninety percent, which showed the rough bridge would still stand.

qa.q: How might Mr Fernandes have seen young Asif's redrawing?
qa.a: He likely saw a talented student stuck on perfect and cared enough to set a firm time limit.

grounding: Shows a young adult learning to set time limits, make rough versions, practise small imperfections and seek help for lasting worry.

passage: With three hours left before the film-club submission closed and the editing software crashing every twenty minutes, Amandeep made a decision she'd been practising for weeks. No more perfect cuts. She set a timer for ninety minutes and finished a rough version first, jumpy transition and all. "What if it's ninety percent as good as I want?" she asked her teammate Ujjwal. "Then it's better than a hundred percent of nothing," he said, handing her chai. She rendered it with one shaky shot still in. When she pressed submit, her stomach flipped, then settled. Later that week she admitted to Ujjwal that worry about her work kept her awake most nights, and he walked with her to the student wellbeing office.

qa.q: How long was Amandeep's timer?
qa.a: Ninety minutes.

qa.q: How did Amandeep feel when she pressed submit?
qa.a: Her stomach flipped with nerves, then settled into calm.

qa.q: Why was walking to the wellbeing office a wise step?
qa.a: Because her worry was keeping her awake most nights, which needs real support beyond tricks.

qa.q: What is it like for Ujjwal to hear about the sleepless nights?
qa.a: Ujjwal probably feels concerned and wants to help, so he walks with her.

grounding: Illustrates a young adult choosing good enough under pressure, finishing a rough version and seeking support for ongoing worry.

passage:
Vandana set a timer on her phone for forty minutes and wrote at the top of a page: ROUGH DRAFT, ALLOWED TO BE BAD.
Last semester she'd rewritten the first paragraph of her sociology paper nine times and missed the deadline. This time, in the Delhi university library, she kept going even when sentences felt clumsy.
When the timer rang, she had three ugly pages. Tarun, across the table, raised an eyebrow. "Done already?"
"Done with the rough one." She asked herself the question the counsellor had suggested: what if this is ninety percent as good as perfect? Would anyone fail me? Probably not.
She edited for one hour and submitted two days early. Her chest still felt tight when she clicked Submit.
That evening she booked another session with the college counsellor to keep working on the worry, which hadn't fully gone away.

qa.q: How long was Vandana's timer set for?
qa.a: Forty minutes.

qa.q: How did Vandana feel when she clicked Submit?
qa.a: She still felt anxious, with a tight chest, even though she had finished early.

qa.q: Which strategies helped Vandana finish this time?
qa.a: A time limit, a rough draft allowed to be bad, and asking what would happen if the work were ninety percent as good.

qa.q: How might Tarun see Vandana's quick rough draft?
qa.a: Tarun was surprised she was done so fast, perhaps not knowing the rough draft was a deliberate step to beat perfectionism.

grounding: Shows a young adult using a time limit, a rough first version and a good-enough question, and seeking counselling for lingering anxiety.
